name: parr-flash-council-office
prompt: Vertical snapshot, noon, the public waiting area of a shabby present-day English town hall housing desk. Beige walls, a long fake-wood counter with chipped trim, a red ticket machine on a chrome stand showing number 47, a wire rack of bleached pamphlets about bin collections and benefits, a bolted row of orange moulded seats, a dented water cooler, grey carpet squares with a coffee stain. Lined up single file before the counter is a gang of five, patient as pensioners waiting to be called, faces tilted upward in unison. Behind the desk, filling every inch, towers a monstrous pile of loose printed sheets that pushes up through a gap in the suspended ceiling where a polystyrene panel has been shoved aside and hangs crooked off its metal grid; sellotaped to the pile at head height is a single plastic-sleeved A4 page, black capitals on white: THE RULES. Every gang member wears a knitted full-face balaclava, each a clashing shade: acid lime, candy pink, hazard orange, cobalt, canary yellow. The knit is unbroken, with no openings for eyes, nostrils or lips. A wide band of white stitching loops all the way round the front of each hooded head like a halo seen face-on, and in its upper right as we look at them, the person's own left side, roughly two o'clock and well off-centre, a rounded red triangle is sewn on. Below the masks: shiny nylon trackies, a supermarket kagool, a padded jacket, collars zipped high so no neck shows, sleeves down past the wrists, cheap woolly gloves on all ten hands, no skin visible at all. The one at the front clutches a numbered paper ticket. Camera at waist height, square on to the counter, a wide 28mm lens a few paces back, everything in sharp focus front to back, the frame crammed with clutter right to its edges. Light comes from a single blunt flash mounted on the camera, bleaching the counter's veneer into a white hotspot, making the woollen colours shout, dropping a hard-edged black shadow behind each figure on the beige wall, with the far corners of the room sinking a little dimmer. The colour of a slow, punchy negative film printed at a high-street lab: overripe, a bit vulgar, grain visible. Unposed, flat-faced, matter-of-fact comedy.
